newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia says has no preference in U.N. vote.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia says has no preference in U.N. vote.

text.p: Indonesia said on Thursday it has no preference at present among the African candidates in the race for a new U.N. secretary-general.
Foreign Minister Ali Alatas said Indonesia, a member of the U.N Security Council, had supported incumbent Boutros Boutros- Ghali until it became clear he faced a veto on his re-election.
Indonesia now supports an African to replace Boutros-Ghali, Alatas told journalists at the annual foreign ministers' meeting of the 54-member Organisation of the Islamic Conference (OIC) in Jakarta.
Asked if he had any preference among the four African candidates, he replied: "No, at this stage. I think we are just in the straw polling vote where we don't have any preference yet."

The 15-member Security Council on Tuesday and Wednesday held five rounds of informal voting meant to "discourage" or "encourage" four declared candidates from Africa, which is given preference in fielding nominees.
It will resume unofficial voting on Thursday.
One of the candidates is Hamid Algabid of Niger, who was succeeded as secretary-general of the OIC on Thursday by former Moroccan prime minister Azeddine Laraki after an eight-year term.
British Foreign Secretary Martin Rifkind sent an "urgent message" to Alatas on Wednesday in which he urged support with the Security Council for Ghana's Kofi Annan, who himself faces a French veto.
Rifkind said in his message, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, that he regarded Annan as the strongest candidate for the top U.N. post.
"I believe it would be in the best interests of the Security Council and of the U.N. as a whole if the council could come together in support of him," Rifkind said.
Alatas, asked if Indonesia had come under pressure over the vote, replied: "No. I think everything is still at a preliminary stage."
The other candidates are Ivory Coast Foreign Minister Amara Essy and Amadou Ould-Abdallah of Mauritania.
No formal vote has been held since the United States vetoed Boutros-Ghali on November 19 while the other 14 council members supported him. His five-year term expires on December 31.
Washington contends Boutros-Ghali, a former Egyptian deputy prime minister, is too weak in reforming the world body, a position shared by few other countries.
Boutros-Ghali suspended his candidacy on December 4 and could reactivate it at any time. But he is believed certain to be vetoed again by the United States.
